title: You didn’t expect the weakness to stay this long.
paragraphs: You didn’t expect the weakness to stay this long.

You prayed about it.
You fasted.
You tried to outgrow it, out-discipline it, outfaith it.
But it’s still there.

That quiet ache.
That recurring struggle.
That thing you thought God would’ve taken away by now.

And you’ve started to wonder…
“If God is with me, why won’t He remove this?”
That question isn’t new.
The man who wrote half the New Testament asked it first.
“Because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh… Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:7–8
Paul wasn’t weak in the way you think.

He saw heaven.
He carried revelation most people couldn’t even comprehend.
God used him with power, authority, miracles.
And still… he had a thorn.

Not a small inconvenience.
Not a passing discomfort.
A thorn.
Something that stayed. Something that hurt. Something that followed him.
And here’s what most people don’t realize…
That thorn wasn’t an accident.
“…a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.” — 2 Corinthians 12:7

God allowed what Paul hated…
to protect what God was building.
Read that again.

You’ve been asking God to remove something
He’s using to save you from something worse.

Because pride doesn’t feel like a threat when you're in pain.
Dependence doesn’t grow when everything is easy.
And surrender doesn’t deepen when you’re always comfortable.
God saw it.

He saw what Paul could become if everything went unchecked.
He saw how revelation without restraint could destroy him.
So He didn’t remove the thorn.
He repurposed it.
And Paul begged.

Not once. Not casually.
Three times.
He asked God to take it away.
And heaven responded—but not the way he wanted.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9
That’s the lesson.

Not that God always removes pain.
But that He transforms its purpose.

You wanted deliverance.
God is offering dependence.

You wanted escape.
God is building endurance.

You wanted relief.
God is forming Christ in you.

You knew something wasn’t changing…
but you didn’t understand why.
Now you’re starting to see it.

The thing you’ve been fighting might be the very place
God is teaching you to rely on Him.
Because grace is not just forgiveness.
It is sustaining power.

It’s what holds you together
when the thorn is still there.

It’s what strengthens you
when your strength runs out.

It’s what keeps you grounded
when everything in you wants control.
Paul’s response shifts here.

He stops asking for removal
and starts embracing the purpose.
“Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9
That doesn’t mean he enjoyed the pain.
It means he finally understood it.
Weakness wasn’t disqualifying him.
It was positioning him.

Because when you stop pretending you’re strong,
that’s when God’s power actually shows up.
But there’s something deeper.
The thorn also exposes something in you.

Your limits.
Your hidden fears.
Your need for control.
Your struggle to trust God fully.
And beneath all that…
Sin.

Not always in the obvious sense.
But in the quiet resistance.

The part of you that still wants life your way.
The part that doubts God’s goodness when He says “no.”
The part that believes comfort is better than transformation.
That’s where the Gospel steps in.
Because your greatest problem isn’t the thorn.
It’s the separation sin created between you and God.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
That’s why Jesus came.

Not just to remove discomfort…
but to rescue your soul.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Jesus didn’t avoid suffering.
He embraced it.
He took the weight of sin, the wrath you deserved, the punishment you couldn’t carry…
And He didn’t ask for the cross to be removed.
He submitted to it.

So that through His death…
you could receive life.

Through His weakness…
you could receive strength.

Through His sacrifice…
you could receive grace.
That same grace is what meets you in your thorn.

Not to leave you stuck—
but to draw you closer.

To strip away your illusion of control.
To anchor you in Christ.
To teach you that He is enough.
So now the question changes.
Not “Why won’t God take this away?”
But…
“Will you trust Him while it remains?”
Because one path leads to bitterness, striving, and distance from God.
The other leads to surrender, transformation, and deeper intimacy with Christ.
And you already feel the tension between those two.
If this hit something in you, don’t ignore it.
Say it plainly—“I’ve been fighting what God is using.”
You’ll need it again on the days it hurts more.
